description:
Wesam Saad concludes the disputed-gifts discussion by examining tongues and explaining why he believes the gift has ceased. He begins with concern for the church’s unity and protection from misleading teaching. His first comparison is between the practices he critiques and the intelligible foreign languages described in Acts 2. He argues that these were languages the speakers had not learned, rather than unintelligible utterances. Reading 1 Corinthians 13:1–2 together, he treats the reference to angelic tongues as hypothetical language emphasising the necessity of love. He then connects Acts with 1 Corinthians 14 through interpretation, orderly participation and the church’s edification.

The next argument concerns purpose. Wesam reads Paul’s quotation of Isaiah 28 as describing a sign of judgement towards unbelieving Israel in its historical setting, and relates the use of other languages to worship extending beyond Israel. He regards that purpose as fulfilled and therefore no longer requiring the gift. A further argument returns to the completed canon: if a message is truly God-breathed, he says it carries divine authority and truthfulness. These conclusions remain his interpretation of the passages considered. Listeners are urged to test claims by Scripture rather than experience alone. The closing answer suggests an early cessation, without establishing an exact date.

questions.question: What does Wesam identify as the nature of biblical tongues?
questions.answer: He describes the gift as speaking an intelligible human language that the speaker has not learned. He points to the hearers in Acts 2 recognising their own languages. His comparison therefore distinguishes a language unknown to a particular listener from utterances that cannot be understood as language.

questions.question: How does he interpret the reference to tongues of angels in 1 Corinthians 13?
questions.answer: Wesam reads the first two verses together, comparing tongues with the hypothetical possession of all mysteries and knowledge. He argues that Paul is using an extreme supposition to show that even extraordinary ability is worthless without love. He does not read the passage as establishing unintelligible angelic speech for Christians to practise.

questions.question: Why does he connect the tongues in Acts with those in 1 Corinthians 14?
questions.answer: He notes the shared language terminology, the ability to interpret the speech, the Holy Spirit as its source and comparable reactions from outsiders. In his argument, these features point to the same kind of gift rather than a different, unintelligible language appearing in Corinth.

questions.question: What limits does he read in 1 Corinthians 14 for public use of the gift?
questions.answer: Wesam emphasises two or three speakers at most, one at a time, with interpretation. He also understands the instructions concerning women as excluding their tongues-speaking in that church setting. These are parts of his comparison between the ordered biblical practice he describes and the modern practices he critiques.

questions.question: Why does he question a report that listeners understood a message without the speaker using their language?
questions.answer: Wesam returns to Acts 2, where some hearers recognise the languages being spoken while others do not understand. He argues that the reported situation does not match his reading of the gift, because Acts describes hearers recognising the actual language being spoken, rather than merely receiving the meaning of speech in a language they do not know.

questions.question: How does he interpret tongues as a sign for unbelievers?
questions.answer: Wesam follows the quotation in 1 Corinthians 14 back to Isaiah 28. He reads the foreign-language warning there as judgement upon unbelieving Israel and understands that background as identifying the unbelievers in Paul’s argument. On that reading, tongues carry a warning of judgement rather than functioning chiefly as a private devotional experience.

questions.question: Why does he argue that the gift’s purpose no longer requires its continuation?
questions.answer: Wesam connects the foreign languages with a historical sign of judgement and the extension of worship among the nations. He regards that sign-purpose as accomplished and reasons that the gift is therefore no longer needed. He grounds this conclusion in the gift’s purpose rather than an exact historical cessation date.

questions.question: How does the completed-canon argument enter the discussion of tongues?
questions.answer: Wesam asks whether a claimed message is invented or genuinely God-breathed. If it is God-breathed, he argues that it must carry divine authority and freedom from error. He therefore connects his rejection of continuing revelatory tongues with the earlier argument that the biblical canon is complete.

questions.question: Does the closing discussion establish exactly when tongues ceased?
questions.answer: Wesam suggests that the gift may have ceased during the apostolic period, drawing attention to its place in early accounts and its absence from the later instructions he discusses. He offers this as an inference about its fulfilled purpose. He does not identify a precise cessation date.
